## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
According to the traditional opening framing narrative, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana with reference to a co-resident pupil of Sāriputta [SuttaCentral].
The central narrative concerns a servant named Nanda who holds the secret to where his late master buried a hoard of treasure [Anandajoti 2010]. When taking the deceased master's son to the location, the servant's awareness of possessing this secret makes him arrogant, prompting him to verbally abuse the heir and refuse to point out the wealth [Anandajoti 2010]. In his discussion of early legal and moral terminology, Kanai Lal Hazra observes that the text of Jātaka 39 employs the term *vinaya* in the sense of a moral code of discipline, commending one who properly comprehends conduct and logic [Hazra 1994]. The verse collection of the Jātaka includes *Nandajātakam* among the early single-verse narratives [Anandajoti 2010].
No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan collections are reported on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral]. Similarly, DharmaNexus detects no significant Pali-internal text reuse or external text alignments for this narrative [DharmaNexus].
